data.title: Sebi plans tighter tenure caps for exchange MDs, public interest directors
data.description:
The Securities and Exchange Board of India (Sebi) on Friday proposed a series of governance changes for market infrastructure institutions (MIIs) such as stock exchanges, clearing corporations and depositories.
 
The proposed changes include lower age and term limits for public interest directors (PIDs), a 12-year cap on the combined tenure of managing directors across MIIs, and a board seat for the Association of Mutual Funds in India's (AMFI's) chief executive at the repo clearing corporation.
 
The regulator has proposed cutting the maximum age of PIDs from 75 to 70 years and the cap on terms from three to two. A PID would serve two terms of three years each across MIIs.
 
 
The regulator said the role is quasi-regulatory and more demanding than that of an ordinary non-executive director, and that a narrow pool of individuals can circulate between MIIs.
 
Further, Sebi has proposed that a single term of a managing director (MD) would not exceed five years, with a maximum of two terms and eight years in one MII.
 
Across MIIs, an MD could serve three terms and 12 years in total. Those already serving as MDs would get a 15-year overall ceiling.
 
At present, an MD can serve 10 years in one MII and again at another, with no overall limit.
 
For executive directors (EDs), Sebi proposed eight years in a single MII and 16 years across MIIs.
 
As ED and MD together, the limits would be 12 years in one MII and 20 years across MIIs. Incumbent PIDs, MDs and EDs would continue until their ongoing terms end.
 
“Limits on MD tenure address key man risk. At the same time, staff of MIIs who aspire to senior executive positions should see a credible and orderly path to growth. A ceiling of 8 years as ED in a single MII, with a combined ceiling of 12 years as ED and MD, allows a career path to the top while keeping all executive tenures within known bounds,” noted Sebi.
 
PIDs may also be barred from simultaneous directorships in associates of MIIs, which are currently outside the restriction.
 
Sebi said this closes a structuring gap. The cap on statutory committee memberships per PID would be fixed at four, from the present five.
 
Sebi also proposed that AMFI's chief executive may be appointed, ex officio, to the board of AMC Repo Clearing Ltd (ARCL), which began operations in July 2023.
 
To manage conflicts, the AMFI chief would not sit on the risk management, members or regulatory oversight committees, would recuse themselves from decisions on risk parameters and default management, and would have no access to participant-level data. The appointment would be linked to further capital contribution by AMCs.

data.title: Working on zero wastewater discharge projects: Ecolab's Mukul Girotra
data.description:
Ultra-pure water maker Ecolab is working on several pilot projects that can cut industrial wastewater discharge to zero, especially from technologically complex industries such as semiconductor chip fabrication and electronics manufacturing, said the company's senior vice-president and general manager of the global high tech division, Mukul Girotra, said.
 Though several other projects, such as crystallisers and distillers, have achieved zero-water discharge, Ecolab aims to cut the cost of such projects as low as possible, Girotra said.
 Ecolab is working with several leading semiconductor companies on such projects and is looking to bring the learnings to India so an ecosystem for ultra-pure water is up and running as more chip fabrication projects come to the country, he said.
 Ultra-pure water usage, he said, is lower in projects that work on legacy-node silicon chip fabrication than in leading-edge chip fabrication units, Girotra said, adding that a decent-sized chip fabrication unit consumes roughly 8 million gallons of water per day.
 “For example, in leading-edge plants, you have close to 750 steps from start to finish before the chip is shipped out for packaging. Ultra-pure water is used at every step, after the deposition of every layer. For legacy-node projects, there are about 250 steps involved, so naturally the water usage is less,” he said.
 In addition to working on pilot projects that bring wastewater discharge to zero at the least possible cost, Ecolab is also working on steps to reuse and repurpose ultra-pure water as many times as possible, Girotra said.
 “There are 18 steps involved in manufacturing ultra-pure water, made from the same utility water. Now, the question is, do we let this water go out to discharge after one use? The old philosophy was to use ultra-pure water, treat it and then discharge it. Now, we use, treat, recover, reuse, and then treat and reuse again,” he said.
 Though using water is the best option for heat management in both semiconductor chip fabrication and data centres in tropical countries such as India, companies in this space will have to reduce consumption to a bare minimum through efficient recycling and reuse, he said.
 “We can use other products such as glycol, but using water is nearly 11-17 per cent more efficient in heat transfer and management,” Girotra said.

data.title: Bank of Maharashtra explores AMC business, overseas bond issue: MD & CEO
data.description:
State-owned Bank of Maharashtra (BoM) is exploring opportunities to expand into the wider financial services sector, including setting up an asset management company (AMC), its Managing Director and Chief Executive Officer (MD & CEO), Nidhu Saxena, said on Thursday.
 
In December last year, the government completed a 6 per cent stake sale in the lender, reducing its holding to 73.60 per cent from 79.60 per cent.
 
Speaking on the sidelines of the CII-DFS Financing Summit, Saxena said, “We are looking at potential opportunities to grow in the wider financial sector, including the AMC business.”
 
Separately, the lender is exploring raising up to $175 million through overseas bonds before the Reserve Bank of India’s (RBI’s) concessional swap window for Overseas Foreign Currency Borrowings (OFCBs) closes on December 31, 2026. The decision will depend on prevailing overseas market rates and movements in US Treasury yields.
 
 
“We are exploring the possibility of one more transaction of perhaps $175 million at most. However, we will take a call depending on how the pricing works out,” he said.
 
The bank had earlier raised $500 million through five-year senior unsecured fixed-rate notes carrying a coupon of 6.112 per cent, payable semi-annually.
 
On its GIFT City operations, Saxena said the bank’s International Banking Unit (IBU) had built a business book of around $2 billion in its first year, surpassing its initial target of $1 billion. The lender sees opportunities to raise international resources through GIFT City and expand banking services for non-resident Indians (NRIs), he added.
 
Saxena also stressed the need for alternative funding sources, including equity and debt markets, to finance India’s infrastructure requirements as the country works towards its goal of becoming a developed nation by 2047. While banks would continue to play a key role, traditional lending alone may not be sufficient to meet the country’s growing capital requirements, he said.

data.title: Anthropic shares tumble after record IPO as AI trade faces reality check
data.description:
Anthropic's much-hyped arrival on Wall Street fizzled out on Friday, as a dramatic unravelling of the AI trade showed that even a blockbuster listing could not shake the gloom hanging over the sector.
 
Widely seen as a proxy for the AI trade, Anthropic's listing had been viewed as a potential boost for an industry struggling to regain its footing after a turbulent stretch.
 
But the stock was last trading at $88.24, about 9 per cent below Thursday's close, while losses across other technology heavyweights suggested the IPO had done little to reverse the broader selloff.
 
"Investors still believe in AI but are becoming more selective about what they will pay for that growth," said David Miller, chief investment officer at Catalyst Funds.
 
 
Among the Magnificent Seven stocks, Nvidia and Meta Platforms fell more than 3 per cent each, while Amazon and Microsoft dropped 2 per cent and 1 per cent, respectively.
 
Chip stocks also slid, with AMD and Sandisk down over 6 per cent each and Intel losing more than 3 per cent.
 
The focus now shifts to a potential OpenAI listing, which would be another major test of investors' appetite for AI stocks. OpenAI has indicated it may go public next year.
 
Despite a pipeline of high-profile AI and infrastructure companies, many have pushed their IPO plans to 2027.
 
PATIENCE MAY PAY
 
Anthropic's stock could find support later in the year. London-based index rebalance analytics firm Intropic estimates index-tracking funds could account for purchases of up to 30 per cent of Anthropic's shares by year-end.
 
Near-term volatility, however, could persist as the initial euphoria around the listing fades and investors assess whether a valuation of about 40 times sales over the past 12 months can be sustained.
 
"We favour patience on Anthropic and recommend evaluating the company as it reports public results," said Kaush Amin, head of private market investing at US Bank Asset Management, adding that the current valuation "assumes years of rapid growth."
 
The debut has also done little to ease broader concerns about the health of the AI trade. Wall Street's main indices ended sharply lower on Thursday, while futures pointed to further declines on Friday.
 
PARALLELS WITH SPACEX
 
Anthropic's IPO has drawn parallels with Elon Musk's SpaceX, which went public in June after the second-biggest IPO on record.
 
Anthropic raised $93.5 billion in its IPO after underwriters exercised an option to buy additional shares, surpassing SpaceX's $85.7 billion haul to become the biggest listing on record.
 
While the companies have different business models, some investors have pointed to SpaceX's sharp swings in the weeks after its debut as a reason for caution over buying Anthropic immediately after its listing.
 
"There's going to be some volatility like we had with SpaceX. A lot of people are going to have FOMO. I don't think there's any need to get on it on the first trade," said Rob Hackel, CEO of financial advisory and brokerage firm RF Lafferty & Co.
 
SpaceX shares fell more than 6 per cent.
 
Retail investors traded about $772 million of Anthropic shares on Thursday, the most for an IPO debut since Vanda Research began tracking the data in 2012.
 
The stock's sharp swings have left investors weighing whether to bet on a rebound or brace for further losses. Options trading, due to begin next week, could add to the volatility.
 
"It's not a good environment for Anthropic at the moment," said Carsten Hesse, head of index events at Berenberg.

data.title: Cash transfers near ₹4 trn in FY27 as states expand direct welfare schemes
data.description:
Direct cash transfer schemes may have yielded political dividends for many states, but they are coming at a considerable fiscal cost.
 
Once seen as targeted welfare interventions, they have become among the fastest-growing components of state government expenditure, accounting for a rising share of revenue receipts and reshaping budget priorities.
 
From putting money in the hands of women and farmers to providing income support to youth and vulnerable households, states are committing larger sums to direct transfers, with the combined allocation for 128 identified unconditional cash transfer (UCT) schemes touching nearly ₹4 trillion in 2026-27.
 
According to the recent State of State Finances 2026-27 report by PRS Legislative Research, spending on subsidies and transfers increased from 16 per cent of states' revenue receipts in 2018-19 to 21 per cent in 2023-24, with transfers growing at an annualised rate of 24 per cent, twice the growth rate of subsidies. The share of unconditional cash transfers alone is estimated to rise from 0.6 per cent of GDP in FY23 to 1 per cent in FY27.
 
 
Women and social security pensioners account for almost 90 per cent of the proposed spending, reflecting a marked shift in welfare priorities towards putting money directly into the hands of households rather than relying solely on conventional subsidies and public provisioning.
 
West Bengal has emerged as the largest spender on unconditional transfers, with a combined allocation of ₹47,542 crore, followed by Karnataka at ₹40,392 crore and Maharashtra at ₹38,549 crore. In West Bengal, the total unconditional transfer allocation is higher than the state's capital outlay of ₹40,930 crore.
 
Andhra Pradesh, Telangana and Madhya Pradesh have also made substantial provisions, at ₹33,943 crore, ₹32,629 crore and ₹32,059 crore, respectively. Among other major states, ₹19,036 crore has been provisioned by Tamil Nadu, ₹18,415 crore by Odisha, ₹18,146 crore by Rajasthan and ₹16,450 crore by Kerala.
 
Women account for the largest share
 
Women have emerged as the principal beneficiaries of the new wave of unconditional transfers. West Bengal leads the country with an allocation of ₹36,000 crore for women in 2026-27, followed by Karnataka at ₹28,608 crore and Maharashtra at ₹26,500 crore. Madhya Pradesh ranks fourth with ₹23,883 crore, while Tamil Nadu, Jharkhand and Odisha have earmarked ₹14,414 crore, ₹14,066 crore and ₹10,145 crore, respectively.
 
Punjab, with an allocation of ₹9,300 crore, ranks eighth, ahead of Bihar at ₹9,052 crore, Chhattisgarh at ₹8,200 crore, Haryana at ₹6,500 crore, Delhi at ₹5,110 crore and Assam at ₹3,700 crore.
 
States have launched different schemes based on their respective allocations. While it is Lakshmir Bhandar in West Bengal and Gruha Lakshmi in Karnataka, the scheme is known as Ladki Bahin in Maharashtra and Ladli Behna in Madhya Pradesh. Odisha's Subhadra scheme, Tamil Nadu's Magalir Urimai Thogai and Jharkhand's Maiyan Samman Yojana are also part of this expanding network of women-focused assistance.
 
The schemes have gained prominence since 2023. Madhya Pradesh's Ladli Behna, Karnataka's Gruha Lakshmi and Tamil Nadu's Magalir Urimai Thogai were introduced that year, followed by major initiatives in Maharashtra, Odisha and Jharkhand in 2024. Punjab introduced a women-focused unconditional transfer scheme in 2026-27, while Kerala and West Bengal have increased allocations to their existing programmes.
 
The report pointed out that West Bengal and Jharkhand are spending an estimated 11 per cent and 10 per cent of their revenue receipts, respectively, on women-focused transfers, the highest proportions among states. West Bengal also topped the states in terms of overall direct cash transfers, accounting for around 15 per cent of revenue receipts, followed by Andhra Pradesh and Telangana at 14 per cent, Karnataka and Jharkhand at 13 per cent, and Rajasthan at 12 per cent.
 
Telangana leads farmer assistance
 
The distribution of farmer-oriented transfers presents a different picture. Telangana has made the highest allocation at ₹18,000 crore, substantially ahead of Andhra Pradesh, which ranks second with ₹6,600 crore. Maharashtra follows with ₹6,060 crore, Madhya Pradesh with ₹5,501 crore and West Bengal with ₹5,425 crore.
 
Odisha has earmarked ₹2,030 crore, while Rajasthan has provided ₹1,974 crore. Chhattisgarh's allocation stands at ₹600 crore. The allocations are for direct farm income support in states where agricultural households face uncertain earnings, rising input costs and vulnerability to weather and market fluctuations. Telangana's Rythu Bharosa, Andhra Pradesh's Annadata Sukhibhava, Maharashtra's Namo Shetkari Mahasanman Nidhi and Odisha's CM-Kisan have been supplementing the Centre's PM-Kisan assistance with their own programmes.
 
Such transfers provide farmers with a predictable source of additional income, although their effectiveness in addressing structural agricultural distress depends on whether they are accompanied by investments in irrigation, storage, market infrastructure and better price realisation, the report stated.
 
Pensions remain a major component
 
While women-focused schemes dominate the political discourse around cash transfers, social security pensions account for an equally significant part of state welfare commitments.
 
The PRS report estimates that social security pensions will account for around 0.39 per cent of GDP in 2026-27, compared with 0.5 per cent for women-focused transfers. Farmer assistance accounts for approximately 0.12 per cent and youth transfers just 0.01 per cent.
 
Fourteen states have budgeted to spend more than three-fourths of their total UCT allocation on social security pensions. In Gujarat, Uttar Pradesh and Meghalaya, pensions account for almost the entire unconditional transfer expenditure.
 
Andhra Pradesh leads the states with ₹27,343 crore, followed by Rajasthan with ₹16,172 crore, Telangana with ₹14,629 crore, Kerala with ₹14,500 crore, Uttar Pradesh with ₹13,604 crore and Karnataka with ₹11,184 crore.
 
In contrast, women-focused schemes constitute the majority of UCT spending in Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand, Karnataka and Tamil Nadu. Transfers are generally disbursed monthly in most women-centric schemes, whereas programmes such as Odisha's women and farmer assistance schemes provide money in two or three instalments annually.
 
Youth receive a relatively small share
 
Direct cash assistance to young people remains a much smaller component of state welfare spending. Only five states have specific allocations, with West Bengal leading at ₹2,020 crore, followed by Karnataka at ₹600 crore, Haryana at ₹370 crore and Assam at ₹119 crore. Tamil Nadu has allocated ₹8 crore. West Bengal's allocation is significant, accounting for a large share of the total spending identified for youth across states.
 
The relatively small allocations indicate that governments have been more inclined to use direct transfers to support women and farmers than to provide unconditional assistance to youth.
 
The 16th Finance Commission has already flagged the growing fiscal burden associated with unconditional transfers, particularly where beneficiary coverage is large and targeting is weak.
 
In its assessment, the Commission observed that unconditional transfer schemes tend to have a large and untargeted beneficiary base and can impose a substantial fiscal burden. It recommended rationalising beneficiary coverage to improve the efficiency of expenditure.
 
Amarendra Das, associate professor at the National Institute of Science Education and Research (NISER), said UCTs are not confined to one political party or region. Governments across the country have adopted direct benefit transfers for women, farmers and vulnerable sections, including elderly people, widows and persons with disabilities. But the scale and composition of spending vary considerably, depending on the political priorities and social protection framework of individual states, he added.

data.title: Sebi proposes removing additional disclosure framework for FPIs
data.description:
In a bid to attract more foreign portfolio investors (FPIs) to India, the Securities and Exchange Board of India (Sebi) on Friday proposed removing the Additional Disclosure Framework (ADF) for such overseas investors, which was introduced in August 2023 for granular disclosure on ultimate beneficial owners.
 
This comes against the backdrop of large FPI outflows which have exerted severe pressure on the foreign exchange market and the value of the Indian rupee.
 
Sebi noted that such disclosure requirements may act as “entry barriers” for FPIs and need to be weighed against the prevailing requirements in other jurisdictions “competing for the same pool of global monies”.
 
 
“The granular disclosure requirements under ADF have been prescribed by Sebi over and above the BO (beneficial owners) identification requirements specified under PMLR (Prevention of Money Laundering (Maintenance of Records) Rules, 2005). Further, such granular disclosure requirements under the ADF are unique to India,” the regulator noted.
 
Under the current requirements, if FPIs meet specified concentration or size criteria, they are mandated to submit granular details of all entities holding any ownership, economic interest or exercising control — on a full look-through basis upto all natural persons without any thresholds.
 
These include FPIs that hold more than 50 per cent of their Indian equity assets under management (AUM) in a single corporate group, or those whose individual or combined holdings with their investor group exceed ₹50,000 crore in Indian equity markets.
 
The threshold was raised from ₹25,000 crore to ₹50,000 crore in April 2025. However, exemptions were provided to certain broad-based, pooled funds with diversified investor bases and those with government or government-related ownership, subject to specified conditions.
 
 Under PMLR, the threshold for controlling ownership is 10 per cent and 15 per cent depending on the legal form of the client — thresholds also applicable to FPIs.
 
Sebi added that several developed markets follow a 25 per cent threshold with lower thresholds only for high-risk entities.
 
“Thus, going by global standards, India follows a more stringent regime for identification of BOs. There may be a need to review the PMLR, 2005 to make it consistent with other jurisdictions. However, this is under the jurisdiction of the Ministry of Finance,” noted Sebi.
 
FPIs have been net sellers in the Indian equity markets for a sustained period starting late 2024 — accelerating in the subsequent years, Sebi noted. It added that while there could have been several factors behind FPI outflows, the “relatively onerous rules” on identification and disclosure of BOs compared to other countries necessitated a review.  
 
“Many foreign investors looking to invest in India consider the granular disclosure requirements as an additional compliance burden. Rather than investing in India and be subject to granular disclosures, many investors may instead choose to avoid investing in India,” noted Sebi.
 
The additional disclosure framework came months after the now defunct Hindenburg Research levelled allegations of violations of minimum public shareholding and stock manipulation against the Adani group — which were denied by the ports-to- retail conglomerate.
 
In its discussions with the FPIs, Sebi noted some of the challenges raised by overseas investors included collecting information from a significantly larger number of underlying investors for India specific investments, requirement to set up different fund for India investments owing to different compliance levels, frequent change in investor holdings in pooled vehicles such as hedge funds, and difficulty in tracing ownership in structures such as fund of funds.
 
“Disclosure requirements that are not in line with globally accepted practices could potentially place India at a competitive disadvantage vis-à-vis peer jurisdictions with relatively lenient regulatory requirements,” noted the paper.

data.title: DP World arm, Cochin Shipyard eye JV for ship repair unit at Vadinar
data.description:
After joining forces for the international ship repair facility in Cochin two months ago, DP World’s subsidiary Dubai Drydocks World (DDW) and state-owned Cochin Shipyard (CSL) are in talks to build and operate another repair facility, according to multiple people familiar with the matter.
 
The two companies had already formed a joint venture for the Cochin ship repair facility in September.
 
They have been in talks on possible structures, required investments and responsibilities for the proposed facility at Vadinar in Gujarat, one of the persons said.
 
The plan for the facility was approved by the Union Cabinet in May, and the repair yard is expected to be built at a cost of ₹1,570 crore.
 
The Vadinar ship repair facility will directly address a critical gap in India’s ship repair infrastructure, as the country currently lacks adequate domestic capacity to repair large vessels exceeding 230 metres in length, the Cabinet had said.
 
“By enabling repair of vessels up to 300 metres, the facility will allow high-value repairs of large vessels within India. This will significantly reduce dependence on foreign shipyards and curb foreign exchange outflow,” it said.
 
The project is expected to generate around 290 direct and around 1,100 indirect jobs across ship repair, logistics, and ancillary industries.
 
Responding to this paper’s queries, DDW said, “Dubai Drydocks World and Cochin Shipyard are currently exploring a potential opportunity related to the development of a shipyard in Vadinar.  Discussions remain at an exploratory stage, and no decision has been taken at this time.”
 
In September, the two companies had entered a ₹1,800 crore deal for the repair facility in Cochin, which was being run solely by CSL prior to that.
 
During the signing, officials had said that the JV model for ships will see growth across the country.
 
“This joint venture shall not be limited to Kochi. It is a replicable model that can be extended across India’s extensive coastline, creating hubs of excellence in ship repair and conversion,” shipping secretary Vijay Kumar had said during the signing of the deal between CSL and DDW.
 
India’s maritime plan till 2047 places major emphasis on ship repair. The Maritime Amrit Kaal Vision 2047 said the ship repair industry in India has not expanded over the years to its potential.
 
India has a favourable location as around 7-9 per cent of global trade passes within 300 nautical miles of the Indian coastline. Hence, a huge potential lies for the country to become a major ship repair hub in the world, it said.
 
Ship repairing in the country is a time consuming process with inconsistent results and reduced efficiency.
 
There is a lack of availability of spares within the country as the majority of original equipment manufacturers (OEMs) are located outside India.

data.title: Britain, EU clinch food and youth deals, but are stuck on tuition fees
data.description:
Britain and the European Union sealed deals on easing food trade and boosting youth mobility to reset ties at a summit on Friday, but pushed back an agreement on university tuition fees and left open broader discussions about their long-term relationship.
 
A decade after Britain voted to leave the now 27-nation bloc, rancour has faded and both sides have recognised the need for a closer alliance as the world order is reshaped by Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, US tariffs, China's dominance of critical minerals supply chains and war in Iran.
 
"In a more dangerous world, we are stronger together," British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said in a statement on the eve of the summit, a view echoed by European Council President Antonio Costa.
 
 
"We remain open to having the closest possible relationship between the European Union and the United Kingdom," Costa told a press conference at the end of the summit.
 
The two sides concluded agreements on food checks, youth mobility and an emissions trading scheme, but put off for six months a deal on reducing university tuition fees, which the EU wants but Britain has resisted.
 
Burnham, who was greeted on arrival by a string quintet, has said Britain should consider options for its future relationship, including rejoining the EU. On Monday, he said it was an "obvious truth" that Britain had lost more than it had gained from Brexit.
 
"I think we can all confidently say this is a good day for Britain and this is a good day for Europe," Burnham told a press conference after the summit. "The agreement that we've reached together is a win-win," he said, adding that it would cut costs and benefit consumers.
 
At the summit, postponed from July after the resignation of Burnham's predecessor Keir Starmer, the two sides addressed a small part of those Brexit losses with a package of agreements.
 
The most significant allows cross-border trade in animals, plants and related products, such as sausages or seeds, without the certificates and controls currently required. Britain has estimated this could add up to £5.1 billion ($6.7 billion) per year to its economy.
 
A further agreement will link the emissions trading systems of Britain and the EU, which would exempt British and EU goods, such as steel, from each other's border carbon levies.
 
Each side is also set to allow the other's young people in to work or study for three years, but here divergences are clearer. Britain, mindful that immigration was a factor in the Brexit vote, had proposed letting in only 50,000 but has agreed to 100,000, EU diplomats said.
 
DIVERGENCE ON UNIVERSITY FEES
 
Despite the agreements, some contentious issues remain unresolved, notably the cost of studying at British universities.
 
The two sides continue to differ over tuition fees, with EU countries wanting their students to be eligible for "home fees" at British universities, rather than the international rate, which is typically four times as much.
 
Britain prefers to offer only "significantly reduced" fees, and the aim is now to resolve the issue within six months.
 
The deals are to apply from 2028, with the first young people able to benefit from youth mobility by 2030, a joint summit statement said.
 
Then there is the topic of Britain accepting EU rules, a sensitive issue for opponents of EU membership.
 
A key British demand is that the EU grant it special status under the bloc's "Made in Europe" rules, notably for cars. The EU has indicated it is willing to grant this, but only on condition that Britain align with its policies, which restrict imports of Chinese electric vehicles.
 
The draft joint statement had featured conflicting lines from Britain and the EU about the extent of coordination.
 
The final agreed wording said that, in sectors where cooperation had been agreed, Britain would "ensure outcomes consistent with relevant EU measures" to protect sectors and guard against circumvention.
 
This seems to allude to a Franco-German proposal that EU public money could be spent on British cars, through public procurement or subsidies, if Britain agreed to dynamic alignment with EU trade protection measures.
 
That could mean Britain adopting measures the EU has taken to restrict imports of Chinese-built hybrid and battery-electric vehicles, which London has so far been reluctant to do.

data.title: Threats, insults, settlements: How Jensen Huang made humiliation routine
data.description:
By Emily Steel, Kalley Huang, Ryan Mac and Tripp Mickle
 
As Nvidia became wealthier and wealthier in recent years, Jensen Huang grew increasingly frustrated with his staff.
 
He told groups of subordinates that they had become so rich that he couldn’t motivate them simply with money, according to three people who spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss confidential conversations. The only way he could grind more work out of them, he added, was through humiliation.
 
This was an extension of a philosophy that went back decades. Huang had for years been berating his employees, documents and interviews show. His tongue lashings were savage and inventive. He told one executive that his mother should have aborted him, according to one witness. He said he would rip both arms off a subordinate and beat the person over the head to death with them. And he told another employee he would rip off the top of their head and “pee on your brain.”
 
 
The tirades were a centerpiece of the culture at Nvidia throughout its meteoric rise to a $5 trillion company and cornerstone of the artificial intelligence revolution. They were also foundational to Huang’s management style.
 
“I’d rather torture you into greatness, because I believe in you,” he once said.
 
He has long used humiliation as a tool, excoriating employees in front of their peers with insults, personal attacks and violent comments, while telling them it was good for them or for the business, according to more than a dozen current and former employees, who spoke on the condition of anonymity for fear of reprisal, and to a review of hundreds of pages of court records and other documents spanning more than 20 years. The behavior kept Nvidia’s human resources department busy fielding workplace complaints, but some employees said the department did not take them seriously.
 
Huang also inspired love and reverence from many of his employees. Thousands have signed a letter asking for his return. Some have tattoos of Nvidia’s logo. Both those who liked Huang and those who disliked him described Nvidia as cultish. He cultivated loyalty through not just his technical mastery but also acts of personal compassion and praise. But he ruled through fear.
 
Huang’s behavior began long before Nvidia became one of the most valuable companies in the world. In at least two cases originating in the mid-2000s, the company struck settlements with former senior leaders, both of whom had raised concerns about Huang’s conduct, saying it was unlawful and exposed Nvidia to liability.
 
Michael Winston, a former senior vice president of human resources, threatened to sue Nvidia in 2005, saying that he had been fired after objecting to Huang’s conduct, which he described as “the most verbally abusive, threatening and intimidating behavior” he had witnessed in his career. Huang “thinks he can get away with anything,” Winston wrote in notes he made around that time, which were reviewed by The New York Times.
 
Nvidia reached a confidential settlement agreement with Winston for more than $1 million, which has not been previously reported.
 
Huang resigned from Nvidia last week, after revelations of multiple extramarital relationships, including one with a subordinate and another with a woman whom U.S. intelligence believes to be a Chinese intelligence asset. But his imprint remains on the culture of the company he co-founded in 1993.
 
Some managers followed Huang’s lead, six current and former employees said — including his own daughter, Madison, who as his de facto chief of staff often yelled at people, including executives senior to her. (She continues to work at Nvidia.)
 
Huang denied Winston’s allegations in a statement from his spokesman, John Fisher, saying they are from an employee who was fired. They are “fabrications that are now impossible to disprove specifically, and the thousands of Nvidia employees who continue to speak out for Jensen show they’re false,” Fisher said. Fisher declined to answer other questions regarding Huang’s behavior.
 
Nvidia declined to comment. Its board and Colette Kress, its interim chief executive, must now decide if the company will continue in the mold of Huang or forge a new way forward. She will do so in the face of pressure from Huang and his supporters, who are agitating for his return to the company. Huang once belittled Ms. Kress in a meeting with top executives, The Wall Street Journal reported.
 
Harvey C. Jones, the chair of Nvidia’s board, said Tuesday that it “does not intend to reinstate Jensen as C.E.O.” Earlier this month, the board opened an investigation into Huang.
 
‘It Pained Me’
 
Silicon Valley has a long history of founders and chief executives with caustic management styles. Steve Jobs, the co-founder and chief executive of Apple, was infamous for screaming at and insulting employees who did not meet his exacting standards. He was also beloved. Employees credited his approach with helping to create culture-changing products like the iPod and iPhone.
 
Huang had a similar effect on his staff. He created a flat organizational structure where he interacted with employees at almost every level of the business. He impressed them with his vision for the future of technology, his command of business strategy and the speed at which he tackled and seemed to conquer new areas of importance, leading the company to the forefront of the A.I. boom.
 
Many of the company’s senior leaders have worked for Huang for more than a decade. Some shared Huang’s belief that mediocrity should be stamped out and excellence pursued, said four current and former employees. If employees didn’t like it, they could leave.
 
But in the eyes of some, Huang’s behavior was extreme, even by Silicon Valley standards.
 
In September 2004, Winston joined Nvidia to lead human resources. A longtime human resources executive who previously worked at Merrill Lynch and Motorola, Winston was soon taken aback by the disarray of the H.R. department and the cultural norms of Nvidia. This account of his time at the company is based on interviews and Winston’s notes and emails, as well as drafts of a lawsuit and other legal documents reviewed by The Times.
 
In his first days at Nvidia, he learned that two key human resources leaders had just quit and others were on the verge of resigning.
 
That October, at a two-day off-site meeting attended by about 50 employees, Winston said Huang unleashed graphic violent threats.
 
“You have to do this, or I will rip your fucking heart out and stomp on it,” Huang said at one point.
 
“I watched them helpless, as they were publicly humiliated, indeed tormented, for extended periods of time, by this lunatic!” Winston said in his notes. “It pained me physically, intellectually and emotionally to be in the room.”
 
Winston said other attendees were “terrorized” and pleaded with him to intervene. Days later, he voiced his concerns during a meeting with top executives. One told him that the conduct was typical but could be a liability for the company. Another advised him to “toughen up.”
 
Winston said he then confronted Huang, warning him that he had “crossed the line” and that mistreating employees could expose Nvidia to lawsuits. He said Huang dismissed the concerns and defended public humiliation as a “rite of passage.” Winston said Huang bragged to him that he subjected new employees to it during their first six months at the company to test whether they would stand for it.
 
Winston said Huang told him that he would not stop. “It has good entertainment value,” Huang told him.
 
That November, Winston was called into a meeting with Huang and another executive, who then fired him. Huang told Winston that he was “not a good fit.” If Winston sued Nvidia, Huang said he would make sure Winston never worked in Silicon Valley again.
 
“To say Nvidia fired me because it just was not ‘a fit’ is nothing more than a smokescreen,” Winston said in his notes. “The real issue,” he wrote, was Huang’s “unconscionable behavior.”
 
In the months that followed, Winston filed a formal complaint against Nvidia with California’s Department of Fair Employment and Housing, making allegations that he was fired for opposing Huang’s treatment of employees, including what he said constituted sexual harassment. Winston then drafted a lawsuit against Nvidia and Huang.
 
But before the complaint was filed, both sides reached a settlement. Neither side admitted liability or wrongdoing.
 
Winston rejoined the banking industry, and later blew the whistle against Countrywide Financial Corporation for its conduct during the buildup to the financial crisis. He died earlier this year.
 
In 2007, Stephen Pettigrew, a former lawyer for the company, sued Nvidia over claims that included age discrimination and retaliation for reporting Winston’s allegations of sexual harassment. Pettigrew reported in a complaint filed with the California Department of Fair Employment and Housing that he sought “emergency medical attention for severe nervous tension and anxiety, as a direct result of the actions of Nvidia.”
 
Pettigrew discussed Winston’s complaint during depositions for his own lawsuit, citing Winston’s allegations as evidence of misconduct that exposed Nvidia to legal risk. Nvidia’s general counsel at the time, David Shannon, confirmed during another deposition in the case that Winston’s dispute was resolved in a pre-litigation financial settlement.
 
Nvidia denied all wrongdoing, and said that Pettigrew was fired for poor performance. The company countersued, saying that he breached his contract and misused company documents. The case ultimately settled out of court in 2009.
 
‘Thank You, Jensen’
 
After Nvidia’s chips were used in 2012 to train an early artificial intelligence system, Huang concluded that the future of computing would be A.I. Employees recall receiving his email on a Friday saying the company was pivoting its business from graphics to deep learning, a precursor to A.I. He froze hiring for anybody but experts in that field, and Nvidia became an A.I. chipmaker overnight.
 
A decade later, Huang’s bet paid off when ChatGPT arrived, kick-starting frenzied interest and investment in A.I. Demand for Nvidia’s chips skyrocketed, and the company’s value soared. Many of the company’s 42,000 employees became fabulously wealthy and were exhilarated to be at the forefront of a technology Huang referred to as the next Industrial Revolution.
 
In the wake of Huang’s resignation, some employees have shared stories of a boss who went out of his way to support them. Last week, Vartika Singh, who works on strategy at Nvidia, recalled Huang’s support when her sister had brain cancer.
 
“Thank you, Jensen,” Ms. Singh wrote in a social media post. “For your guidance, for believing in people and ideas long before the rest of us understood them, and above all, for your extraordinary humanity.”
 
Huang’s mix of disparagement and motivation created something akin to Stockholm syndrome, six current and former employees said. The phenomenon, in which somebody held captive develops an emotional bond with their abuser, mirrored their relationship with Huang, they said.
 
Rather than fire people, Huang sometimes preferred to further humiliate them. When Ned Finkle, his former vice president of strategic marketing, faltered in a meeting with a major customer, Huang chewed him out in front of executives from the other company, said two people who spoke anonymously about the private exchange.
 
Huang then named Finkle vice president of external affairs, or government relations. At the time, Huang considered it one of the least important jobs at Nvidia, the two people said. Finkle did not respond to requests for comment.
 
Power Plays
 
Huang’s tirades continued until the end.
 
He usually did not meet one-on-one with subordinates because, he has publicly said, such meetings reduced transparency within Nvidia. But top executives considered the move a power play that gave Huang more control. If anyone disagreed with Huang, they would have to do so in front of a group. Huang could then fire back, ridiculing that person in front of everyone else.
 
Huang also ripped into longtime leaders in front of their own teams, telling them their boss was incompetent and unqualified, two people said.
 
In one instance, Huang went around a room, telling managers he would kill them, according to one person with knowledge of the incident. When he reached a person in their 70s, Huang said that the person was really old and everyone hoped they would drop dead.
 
Huang also made personal attacks. He once made fun of an executive who had taken his children camping and said he needed to find a more committed employee for the job, according to one person. He often mocked another executive for enjoying aviation as a hobby, two people said.
 
In 2019, after Nvidia lost a bid to help build a U.S. government supercomputer, Huang castigated a sales executive in front of government officials for missing out on part of a contract worth hundreds of millions of dollars. The executive then threw his employee badge at Huang, who said he accepted the executive’s resignation on the spot, according to two people with knowledge of the incident.
 
Huang’s behavior rubbed off on other senior leaders at the company, including his daughter, Madison. On one call last year with Nvidia’s marketing team, Ms. Huang repeatedly berated a vice president, who then left the call, according to a recording of the meeting reviewed by The Times.
 
“I’m having an anxiety attack,” the vice president said. “I’m going to drop off. I’m sorry.”
 
Ms. Huang did not respond to requests for comment.
 
As Nvidia became the linchpin of the A.I. boom, Huang’s conduct started to spill outside the company. At Nvidia’s developer conference earlier this year, Huang moderated a panel with business partners, including Arthur Mensch, the chief executive of the French A.I. start-up Mistral.
 
During the panel, Huang interrupted Mensch several times, apparently taking issue with the Mistral chief executive’s French accent, according to two people who watched the talk.
 
“You’re not even speaking human,” Huang said at one point, before another panelist intervened. A spokesman for Mistral declined to comment.
 
Daniel Gutierrez, an A.I. researcher and longtime “Jensen fan” who was watching the panel, said the interaction changed his perspective on Huang.
 
“I thought in the moment, what is happening right now that’s causing you to attack this poor guy?” Gutierrez said. “When all the new stuff happened in the last week, I go, wait a minute now. Maybe Jensen isn’t the guy I thought I revered.”

data.title: Labour unions push for higher wages, job guarantees in FY28 Budget talks
data.description:
Labour-sector stakeholders on Friday sought higher minimum wages, wider social security coverage, stronger employment guarantees and measures to address youth unemployment at a pre-Budget consultation chaired by Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman, according to people aware of the matter.
 
Other proposals included lower goods and services tax (GST) on staffing services, gig worker protections and higher pensions.
 
The Indian Staffing Federation (ISF) proposed cutting GST on staffing and manpower supply services from 18 per cent to 5 per cent, while retaining full input tax credit. It said the current rate raised formal hiring costs by around 13 percentage points, making it less competitive against informal and gig arrangements. The proposed cut could generate 15-20 million additional formal jobs over the medium term, including 1.5-2 million in the near term. The gross tax differential was estimated at ₹28,000 crore, with a lower actual revenue impact after input tax credits.
 
ISF also sought a one-time ₹7,000 employer incentive for hiring skilled young people into their first formal jobs, subject to verified EPF enrolment and retention. It proposed extending the PM Viksit Bharat Rozgar Yojana by two years until July 2029, opening the PM Internship Scheme to companies with an annual turnover of at least ₹100 crore and linking stipend support to formal job conversion. Other demands included a national skilling-to-employment mission focused on placements rather than enrolments and allowing corporate social responsibility funds to finance hostels for migrant and women workers near industrial clusters.
 
The Trade Union Co-ordination Centre (TUCC) sought monthly minimum honorariums of ₹10,000 for ASHA workers, ₹15,000 for Anganwadi workers and ₹12,000 for helpers, along with EPF coverage. It also called for EPFO and ESIC benefits for construction workers, funded through state building and other construction workers' welfare cess funds, and appointment letters, minimum wages and social security for contractual railway goods shed workers. Eligible workers above 60 should receive gratuity and terminal benefits, it said.
 
TUCC proposed doubling the gratuity ceiling from ₹20 lakh to ₹40 lakh and raising the calculation from 15 to 21 days' wages for every completed year of service. It also sought welfare boards for fishermen, street vendors and transport workers, and subsidised EPF and ESIC contributions for eligible micro, small and medium enterprises, with the Centre and states sharing costs equally. Other demands included free family health insurance for lower-income households whose members had paid income tax for five consecutive years.
 
For gig workers, TUCC proposed an aggregator-funded social security fund, health insurance of up to ₹5 lakh and comprehensive accident cover, with registration through e-Shram.
 
The Centre of Indian Trade Unions (CITU) demanded a national minimum wage of ₹42,000 per month, a publicly funded minimum income guarantee of the same amount for those outside regular wage employment and a universal monthly pension of ₹21,000 for the elderly. It also sought restoration of the Old Pension Scheme, repeal of the four labour codes and 200 days of rural employment under the Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Act, alongside an urban employment guarantee.
 
CITU criticised the ₹30,000-crore allocation under the MGNREGS head for 2026-27, against ₹88,000 crore in the previous year's revised estimates.
 
CITU further called for filling vacancies in government departments, semi-government establishments and public-sector undertakings, and time-bound regularisation of eligible contractual workers. Its other demands included a legal guarantee for minimum support prices, stronger public procurement, universal public distribution, healthcare spending of 3 per cent of GDP and education spending of 6 per cent. It also sought protection against job displacement due to artificial intelligence and automation, wealth and inheritance taxes, and higher taxation of extraordinary corporate profits.
 
The Hind Mazdoor Sabha (HMS) also flagged youth unemployment and vacancies in state governments and public-sector undertakings, where many workers were employed on contract. It sought a proposal to fill these posts and a National Wage Policy providing for regular minimum wage revisions in line with inflation and the cost of living, with periodic tripartite reviews. It also proposed raising the income-tax threshold from ₹12 lakh to ₹20 lakh.
 
The Telangana Gig and Platform Workers' Union and the Indian Federation of App-Based Transport Workers sought a dedicated gig worker welfare board, backed by budgetary support and fixed platform contributions for every completed transaction. Citing unpredictable earnings, unsafe conditions, arbitrary rate changes and sudden account blocking, they called for fair payments, transparent platform reporting, safeguards against arbitrary termination and effective grievance redressal. They also flagged opaque algorithm-based management and limited collective bargaining rights, seeking health and accident insurance and pension benefits.
